So, Pedro, tell me about a case that did not go to plan. Everybody has one.
Mine came out of the blue. I was reviewing a supplier renewal on a Friday evening when I noticed a clause that nobody had flagged.
Let me guess. It had renewed automatically.
Exactly. By the time I found it, the contract had already rolled over for three years, and the supplier had been sending invoices at the new price for a month.
That would catch anybody off guard. What did you do?
I spent the weekend trying to piece together the paper trail. The turning point was an old email: their own manager had promised us ninety days of notice.
So it backfired on them. I had a case like that in my second year. It dragged on for eight months because we were arguing about the wrong clause.
Ours came to a head in one meeting. In hindsight, the email was the whole case. We just had not read it.
I was reviewing the contract when I noticed the clause.
By the time we found it, the contract had already renewed.
In hindsight, the answer had been in the paper trail all along.

When I prepare a witness, I tell them the same thing every time: a story is not a list. The mistake almost everybody makes is to tell everything in the order it happened. In March we signed, in April they called, in May we met. By the third date, the jury has stopped listening, because nothing tells them which part matters. So I ask them to start at the moment things changed. I was closing the office on a Friday when the call came. Now everybody is in the room with you. Then you go back. By then, we had already lost two weeks. We had been waiting for that document since January. The tenses do the work for you. One sets the scene, one takes the listener back, and nobody needs a calendar to follow it. A witness who can do that sounds like somebody who was actually there.

The worst week of my career started on a Tuesday. I was sitting in a hotel in Chicago, preparing for a completely different meeting, when my phone rang. Our largest customer had terminated the contract by email the night before, and nobody in the office had seen it. It had gone to an address that nobody had checked since the merger. By the time I landed back home, the team had been working on it for eighteen hours, and they had already found the problem. The notice period had started the moment the email arrived, whether anybody read it or not. We saved the account in the end, but only just. In hindsight, the problem was never the customer. It was the notice clause we had written ourselves, and it had been sitting in our own template for six years.

The supply contract was signed with an automatic renewal clause that nobody flagged. Two years later, the supplier started sending invoices at a new and much higher price. One Friday evening, while he was reviewing the renewal, Pedro noticed the clause. He spent the weekend piecing together the paper trail, and he found an old email promising ninety days of notice. The dispute came to a head in one meeting, and the supplier withdrew the invoices that afternoon.
